en-US.shortDescription: Keeps a family caring for a parent on the same page: stops a second dose, sorts appointments, and says why.
en-US.fullDescription:
When a family looks after a parent, the care is split between a daughter with the doctor's letters, a son in another state, a home aide on weekday mornings, and the parent herself, who sometimes forgets. Nobody holds the whole picture. Hearth gives Alexa+ that picture.

Hearth remembers who said what, when, and whose word counts for which decision. Ada holds Mom's health care proxy, so her rule about medication stands over anyone else's. It keeps the day's record: which dose was given, by whom, at what time. So when Mom goes to take her blood thinner a second time, Alexa says: "Hold on, Rose. Grace gave you today's warfarin at 9:10 this morning. It's once a day, so not another until tomorrow." Hearth makes that refusal itself, from the family's own rule and today's record, and writes it down.

One sentence can do several things. "Mom's cardiology moved to Thursday at ten, sort it out" moves the appointment, works out from the family rota who is taking her, cancels the old ride, books a new one, and tells the family.

It remembers across days and devices. A son who checks in from his own Echo hears only what changed since he last asked, including anything Alexa stopped.

It explains itself. Ask why, and Alexa names the rule, who set it, when, and why it won over anyone who disagreed. Situations end by themselves too: a rule that only applies while she is on antibiotics stops when someone says the course is finished.

Refills are prepared as an Alexa checkout, inside the spending limit the family set, with a warning if the same thing was ordered this week. Every action is written to a record the family can read, and the record shows if anything has been changed.

Hearth is not a medical device. It follows the rules the family gives it. Open source under the MIT licence.
